report:
Conclusion: Monk’s pepper—*Vitex agnus-castus* (chasteberry)—can probably reduce overall PMS symptoms for some people, especially standardized extracts taken for several cycles, but the benefit is modest and evidence is not definitive. A 2017 systematic review/meta-analysis found VAC preparations beat placebo for PMS symptom reduction, while noting heterogeneity among trials and preparations (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0002937817303198). A randomized multicenter placebo-controlled trial in moderate–severe PMS also reported good tolerability and efficacy for one extract (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19269753/). The EU herbal monograph recognizes well-established use of a specific dry extract for premenstrual syndrome, which supports regulated products rather than arbitrary supplements (https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/documents/herbal-monograph/final-european-union-herbal-monograph-vitex-agnus-castus-l-fructus-revision-1_en.pdf).

Safety: usually mild—nausea, stomach upset, headache, itching, menstrual changes—but avoid in pregnancy/breastfeeding and hormone-sensitive cancers; use caution with dopamine-related medicines and hormonal contraception, and discuss with a clinician if symptoms are severe or suggest PMDD (https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/chasteberry). Practical takeaway: reasonable to try a standardized product for 2–3 cycles with symptom tracking; stop if adverse effects occur and seek care for disabling mood symptoms.
